clue.text: Crazy French soul, this woman

indicators.note: The word names the language to translate into before any letters are taken, so the noun beside it arrives from Paris rather than London.

blocks.note: mad is crazy
ame is the French for soul, its accent dropped as crosswords always drop them

explanation.walkthrough: One word of French is all the clue asks you to know, and the comma is the join: everything before it builds, everything after it defines.
explanation.definitionFit: this woman -> MADAME: the French style of address for a lady, borrowed into English whenever the one in question is being pointed at politely.

clue.text: Ore obtained by worker underground, a trainee

blocks.note: the worker underground is a miner
the clue's own a, taken as the letter
a trainee driver carries L-plates, so L is the crossword's learner

explanation.walkthrough: 'A trainee' looks like the tail of the surface sentence and is really two more chunks of the build, the last of them an L-plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Ore -> MINERAL: ore is rock worth digging for the metal in it, one particular sort of the naturally occurring solids minerals are.

clue.text: Green finger, perhaps, and what the gardener will do in bed

blocks.note: a gardener's work in a flowerbed is to dig
the gardener's task is a short verb for turning over soil; the pronoun standing for the bed tacks straight onto the end of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Green finger' is the definition wearing gardening clothes, which is why the whole clue reads as one unbroken thought about allotments.
explanation.definitionFit: Green finger, perhaps -> DIGIT: a finger is one of the digits, toes being the others, and 'perhaps' owns the fact that it is only an example.

clue.text: Arranges party – with what’s available

definitions.note: MAKES DO is a verb and the definition is the phrase that always follows it - you make do WITH something - so the setter defines the verb by the words it drags along.

blocks.note: to make an arrangement is to arrange it
a do is a party - an office do, a birthday do

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay says 'makes a do' and the surface says 'arranges a party', which are the same sentence; the dash is where the meaning switches to coping.
explanation.definitionFit: with what's available -> MAKES DO: to make do is to manage on the inadequate means to hand, and the idiom is almost never spoken without this tail.

clue.text: Takes over present-day stop-over

indicators.note: Doing a thing over is doing it again from scratch, so the letters in front are built up a second time in some new arrangement.

blocks.note: AD dates the present era - anno Domini, as against BC
the four letters of STOP, done over

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen is the hiding place: 'stop-over' is one real word on the surface and two separate instructions underneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: Takes over -> ADOPTS: to adopt a proposal, a name or a child is to take it on as your own.

clue.text: Fearless Bobby that’ll open the Guardian

indicators.note: What opens a word is the letter it starts with, so only the initial of the name that follows is wanted.

blocks.note: Bobby Darin, who sang Mack the Knife
the opening letter of the paper's name

explanation.walkthrough: The italics are the tell: a newspaper title is being named, and a title is exactly the sort of thing a setter wants one letter of.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearless -> DARING: both are adjectives for someone who will take a risk, DARING putting its weight on going ahead and doing it.

clue.text: Action completely adopting inverted interior design

indicators.note: To adopt is to take another into your own household, so one piece is taken inside the other rather than set beside it.
Inverted means stood on its head, so that piece is read from its last letter back to its first.

blocks.note: pure as an intensifier - pure nonsense, pure luck - means utter
interior design is DECOR, stood on its head

explanation.walkthrough: Both instructions are doing surface duty in a sentence about home makeovers, which is why neither reads as an instruction at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Action -> PROCEDURE: a procedure is the settled way of going about something, so the word names an action by the rules that govern it.

clue.text: Recommend guests get changed around midnight

indicators.note: Guests who get changed come back in different clothes, and letters that change come back in a different order.
Something placed around another wraps it, so the single letter ends up in the middle of the rest.

blocks.note: the six letters of GUESTS, rearranged and parted to let the other letter in
mid-night: the middle letter of NIGHT

explanation.walkthrough: 'Midnight' explains itself once you split it, and the party surface never lets on that it is an instruction rather than an hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Recommend -> SUGGEST: to suggest a course of action is to put it forward for consideration, which is recommending without insisting.

clue.text: Frantically text Posh about test result of where’s it at

indicators.note: Anything done frantically is done with no care for order, so the letters land wherever they land.
To wrap a coat about you is to put it round the outside, so the shuffled letters close over the other piece.

blocks.note: the eight letters of TEXT POSH, shaken up and parted to admit the other piece
a test result comes back as marks

explanation.walkthrough: Posh Spice and a frantic text make a tabloid surface out of a treasure map. Thirteen letters is a long anagram, so the enumeration is half the help.
explanation.definitionFit: where's it at -> X MARKS THE SPOT: the phrase a treasure map uses to name the exact place, so the idiom stands in for the question of location.

clue.text: Tin and silver catch

blocks.note: SN is tin in the periodic table, from the Latin stannum
AG is silver, from argentum

explanation.walkthrough: Two chemical symbols stacked, and both are worth banking: the ones that look nothing like the English word are the ones setters reach for.
explanation.definitionFit: catch -> SNAG: a snag is the hidden drawback in an offer, the answer to 'what's the catch?' rather than anything done with the hands.

clue.text: Ill-advised Greek ‘humor’ showing Asian guerrilla movement

indicators.note: A plan that is ill-advised has gone wrong somewhere, and letters that have gone wrong no longer stand in their proper places.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: Those quotation marks are load-bearing: the British HUMOUR would leave a U spare, so the setter is flagging that he means the American spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Asian guerrilla movement -> KHMER ROUGE: Pol Pot's Cambodian communists, named from the Khmer people and the French word for red.

clue.text: Fixed time around rugged ridges

indicators.note: Turned around is turned back to front, so the pair of words is read from the far end towards the near one.

blocks.note: a jelly that has set is fixed
an era is a stretch of time

explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a container instruction and is not: nothing goes inside anything here, the two chunks are stacked and then spun.
explanation.definitionFit: rugged ridges -> ARETES: an arete is the knife-edge crest left where two glaciers have gouged a mountain from either side.

clue.text: Got plastered?

blocks.note: The surface is the morning after: to get plastered is to get thoroughly drunk.
The setter means the wall. Brickwork given its coat of mortar has been plastered, and the building trade has its own word for that coat.

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart - one phrase, two trades. The question mark is the setter admitting that the whole clue is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Got plastered? -> RENDERED: in building, to render a wall is to face it with a thin coat of mortar, the sense the drinking surface hides.

clue.text: Saul’s home rebuilt as one for the poor

indicators.note: A house put up again out of the same bricks stands in a different shape, which is what has happened to these letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'One' points back at 'home' in the surface and at nothing in the parse: the fodder's own word is being borrowed to make the definition read naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: one for the poor -> ALMSHOUSE: alms are money given in charity, so an almshouse is a dwelling endowed for people who cannot pay rent.

clue.text: Domestic flight

blocks.note: The surface is an airline timetable - a flight that stays inside one country instead of crossing a border.
The builder's sense is the one wanted: an unbroken run of steps from one floor to the next is a flight, and 'domestic' puts it in a house.

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, no letters to move, and the whole clue turns on which industry owns 'flight'. The nine-letter enumeration is what rules out the aeroplane.
explanation.definitionFit: Domestic flight -> STAIRCASE: a run of steps between two floors is a flight, and the house is what makes it domestic rather than an airline's route.

clue.text: Verse omitted from cover song

indicators.note: What is omitted has been left out, so the letter named first goes missing from the word named second.

blocks.note: the cover on a bed is a duvet
V is the standard shortening of verse, the one printed in a hymn book

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover song' is a real thing - a band playing somebody else's hit - and the setter needs the two words pulled apart and pointing opposite ways.
explanation.definitionFit: song -> DUET: a duet is a piece written for two voices, so the general word names it by one of its particular forms.

clue.text: It’s seen amongst beta, lambda and others

indicators.note: To sit amongst things is to sit in the middle of them, so the letters are written out inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: the letters run straight across the join between the two Greek letters, spanning where one word ends and the next begins

explanation.walkthrough: Two genuine Greek letters make a surface that means exactly what it says, which is the best cover a hidden word can hope for.
explanation.definitionFit: and others -> ET AL: short for the Latin et alii, the tag a citation uses to stand for the co-authors it does not bother to list.

clue.text: Closely examine as I weep noisily

indicators.note: It does double duty: it makes the weeping loud enough to count as bawling, and it tells you to trust your ear over the spelling.

blocks.note: the letter I, said out loud, is the organ you look with
to bawl is to weep hard, and BAWL taken by ear is spelt the other way here

explanation.walkthrough: A homophone in two pieces: the letter written I, then a word for crying hard. Neither is spelt the way it is said.
explanation.definitionFit: Closely examine -> EYEBALL: American slang turned the noun into a verb, so to eyeball something is to look it over hard at close range.

clue.text: With windows sealed, say, in hut

indicators.note: The little word is pure placement: what was named before it drops inside the word named after it.

blocks.note: a hut is a shed
to utter a word is to say it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is a verb here, not the crossword's usual 'for example', and the commas around it are there to make you read it the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: With windows sealed -> SHUTTERED: a shuttered house has its wooden shutters closed across the glass, which seals it against the weather.

clue.text: Letter about impolite PM

indicators.note: A scarf worn about the neck goes round the outside, so this word closes over the other one.

blocks.note: tau is the Greek letter, the one that looks like a T
rude is impolite

explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' in a cryptic is very often a Greek one, and there are only two dozen of them - the short ones repay learning.
explanation.definitionFit: PM -> TRUDEAU: two Trudeaus, father and son, have led Canada as prime minister, so the office is named by one family that held it.

clue.text: Most of team gathering at lift

indicators.note: Most of a word is not all of it, so it arrives one letter short at the far end.
A gathering draws people in together, so the short word is taken inside rather than set alongside.

blocks.note: a football side is an eleven, and it loses its last letter here
the little word goes in letter for letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' is the definition, not the lift everyone is gathering by, and that swap is the whole of the misdirection in a six-word clue.
explanation.definitionFit: lift -> ELEVATE: to elevate is to raise something to a higher position, the verb sense of lift rather than the British name for a hoist.

clue.text: Great effort making boot

blocks.note: an informal British expression for really putting your back into something
the everyday short nickname for a rubber wellington boot

explanation.walkthrough: One word, two lives, and the second explains the first: putting your foot into something hard is where the effort sense comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Give it some wellie' is the idiom for real force behind an action, and the same word is the rubber wellington you pull on in the rain.

clue.text: Unrivalled, as the House of Lords in recess

blocks.note: the upper chamber is full of peers, and the wordplay wants one of them
in recess the chamber stands empty, so there are fewer of them there - less, not more

explanation.walkthrough: The parse and the joke are the same thing: send the Lords home and the House is short of peers. 'As' only holds the sentence together.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrivalled -> PEERLESS: a peer is an equal, so having no peer is having no rival - the sense kept alive in 'a jury of your peers'.

clue.text: Cost of maintenance all the way to fortification

blocks.note: up in the sense of right to the end - eat it up, use it up
the keep is the strongest tower of a castle

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay wear castle clothes and the answer is a bill rather than a building; the definition is the three words at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Cost of maintenance -> UPKEEP: upkeep is the money a house, a horse or a car swallows simply to be kept in working order.

clue.text: Tibetan priest leaves US city for instrument

indicators.note: Someone who leaves walks out of the place he was in, so those letters come out of the longer word.

blocks.note: Kalamazoo, Michigan, of the Glenn Miller song
the lama is the Tibetan priest, lodged in the middle of the city

explanation.walkthrough: Kalamazoo is the whole clue: a real Michigan city that happens to have a Tibetan priest sitting inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: instrument -> KAZOO: a kazoo is a toy wind instrument, a short tube with a membrane that buzzes when you hum down it.

clue.text: Dessert Azed rejects, served in a globe

indicators.note: To reject something is to throw it out, and what gets thrown out here is the ED the name ends with.
A dish served is a dish turned out of its mould, and letters turned out land in a fresh arrangement.

blocks.note: the Observer setter's name, minus the ED it ends with
eight more letters of fodder, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: Azed sets the hardest cryptic in Britain, so borrowing his name and then discarding half of it is a setter's private joke at his expense.
explanation.definitionFit: Dessert -> ZABAGLIONE: the Italian pudding of egg yolks, sugar and Marsala whisked over heat into a warm foam and spooned into a glass.

clue.text: Enthusiasm at heart of Maoris’ home

indicators.note: The heart of a thing is its middle, so only the letters at the centre of what follows are taken.

blocks.note: the Maoris' home is NEW ZEALAND, and these four letters are its exact centre

explanation.walkthrough: The country is never named, so you have to supply New Zealand yourself before there is anything to take the heart of.
explanation.definitionFit: Enthusiasm -> ZEAL: zeal is enthusiasm with conviction under it, the word English reaches for when the eagerness is moral or religious.

clue.text: Songs by Schubert suggested by violinist

indicators.note: A thing suggested is called to mind rather than stated, so what is wanted is the word the clue's own word calls up when you hear it.

blocks.note: the leader of an orchestra is its principal violinist, and LEADER is what the answer is heard as

explanation.walkthrough: The German plural is what makes it work: one Lied, many Lieder, and only the plural lands on the orchestra's leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Songs by Schubert -> LIEDER: a Lied is a German art song setting a poem for voice and piano, and Schubert wrote some six hundred.

clue.text: Old England, Peru – new continent

indicators.note: Something made new is made over out of the same material, so these letters are put back together in another order.

blocks.note: O is the standard shortening of old, as in Old English
E is England on a scoreboard or a car plate
four more letters of fodder, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old England' reads as one patriotic phrase and is two separate abbreviations; the dash is where the wordplay stops and the definition starts.
explanation.definitionFit: continent -> EUROPE: one of the handful of great landmasses the world divides into, so the general term is pointing at a particular one.
